masthead_title: Credit spreads widened right along with today's chip-sector selling — for the first time this week, credit stopped staying calm.
regime_line: High-yield and investment-grade credit spreads both widened today (HY OAS to 3.72%, IG OAS to 0.98%, each among the highest readings of the past six months) alongside a second straight session of cap-weighted tech weakness — a reversal from Monday-Tuesday, when the same pattern ran with credit staying calm.

Claims ledger — one expires inconclusive today, one still open and close to resolving

CL-0075 (Monday's Jensen Huang reinstatement rally — NVDA +31%, SMH +15% to $460.18 — marking the start of a genuine reversal, not a one-day relief bounce) — not yet due (2026-12-01), 2 of its 5 test sessions in. SMH has given back most of Monday's gain on both sessions since: Tuesday's close of $426.75 and today's $422.46 sit just $2.46 above the $420 refute line and nowhere near the $480 confirm line. Still open, but the data since Monday has moved toward “relief bounce,” not “durable reversal.”

CL-0076 (Wednesday's Core PCE and preliminary Q3 GDP prints either broadening the chip-sector risk-off case or leaving it sector-specific) — expires inconclusive today, a day ahead of Friday's deadline, since Wednesday's own session is what the test specified and every input is already in hand. Per Benzinga and BigGo Finance, October core PCE printed in line at +0.3% m/m (+3.3% y/y, the highest since November 2023), while the BEA's second estimate revised Q3 GDP up sharply to +4.3% annualized from the +3.4% advance figure — neither clears the confirm bar (PCE at or above +0.4% m/m, or GDP at or below +3.0%) nor the refute bar (PCE at or below +0.2% together with GDP at or above +3.6%, since PCE missed that side too even though GDP cleared it). HY/IG OAS did widen further and the S&P 500 did close below Monday's 7,201.09 reference — so the credit/price half of the confirm test fired (Dashboard, below) — but the growth-and-inflation data itself came in too mixed to call either way. Today's chip-sector weakness (Movers, below) stays unexplained by this particular data pull.
story_html:
Oracle's five-year credit-default-swap spread — in plain terms, the market price of insuring against Oracle defaulting on its debt — hit a record of roughly 356 basis points overnight, per S&P Global Market Intelligence data reported by BigGo Finance and Webull, more than four times where it traded a year ago; the company's 2031 notes reportedly priced to yield near 18%. That single-name extreme landed next to a broader, milder credit move: HY and IG OAS (the extra yield lenders demand on junk and investment-grade borrowers) both widened today, a reversal from Monday-Tuesday's pattern of chip-sector selling with credit staying calm (Concept, below). The state file confirms the shift is real, if modest in basis-point terms: both series now sit among the highest readings of their own past six months (Dashboard, below).

The same day's growth and inflation data landed in between the two readings that would have made the call for the broader market one way or the other: October core PCE printed in line, and the BEA's second look at Q3 GDP came in well above even the strong advance estimate (Claims, above) — strong growth, calm inflation, neither clearly behind today's credit move nor against it. Treasury yields, meanwhile, barely moved and continue to sit at levels last matched broadly in July 2007, just before that cycle's credit stress began in earnest (History, below) — not a new extreme, a persistent one, and one arriving from a much lower policy-rate and inflation starting point than 2007's.
dashboard_interp_html:
Long-end Treasury yields eased again today, continuing a quiet multi-day drift lower, while the curve flattened a touch further. The 3-month bill eased 2bp to 4.34% (z +1.68, flagged — higher than all but a handful of days in the past six months; 54th percentile since the early 1980s, 73rd of the last 30 years). The 2-year eased 2bp to 4.61% (z +0.64, below the flag line; 50th/79th %ile, † a 29-point gap between the two lenses). The 10-year eased 6bp to 4.85% (z +0.17; 45th/81st %ile, †). The 30-year eased 6bp to 5.24% (z −0.01, essentially flat against its own recent range; 46th/80th %ile, † — today's lead History-check fact, below: this level was first reached July 31 and has held on 68 of the 81 sessions since, last matched broadly, before this run, in July 2007). The curve flattened: 2s10s fell 4bp to 24bp (z −1.83, flagged) and 3m10y fell 4bp to 51bp (z −2.26, flagged). Why this matters: a bond is a loan, and the long end barely moving while credit and the dollar did (below) suggests today's story sits in financing conditions and risk appetite, not a fresh read on growth or Fed policy itself.

Credit and the dollar both moved the tighter direction today — a reversal from Monday-Tuesday's pattern, and the real story in this dashboard. HY OAS — the extra yield investors demand to lend to junk-rated companies over safe Treasurys — rose 9bp to 3.72% on its Tuesday-dated print (z +2.79, flagged; 95.5th percentile of its own ~3-year record, marked * since this live series has no multi-decade history, §4F). IG OAS, the investment-grade equivalent, rose 1bp to 0.98% (also Tuesday-dated; z +2.83, flagged; 86.6th percentile of its own ~3-year record, *). A 40-year proxy for investment-grade spreads (Moody's Baa yield minus the 10-year Treasury, used only for direction and timing, never magnitude) still sits at just the 13.7th/10.2nd percentile — genuinely tight on its own long-run terms, a reminder that today's OAS move is a shift off a historically calm base, not a credit market already in distress. The dollar (DXY) eased slightly in price (−0.13% to 103.67) but stayed flagged on its recent run (z +2.08; 75th/84th %ile, †). Gold fell 0.73% to $3,535.80 (z −3.05, flagged) and copper fell 0.56% to $5.33/lb (z −4.10, flagged, this run's largest |z| of any series today for a second straight day — Chart of the day, below), both extending a multi-week decline that looks dollar-driven given DXY's own flag today (Unit 5). Why this matters: yesterday, HY and IG OAS easing while chip stocks fell said the selloff was staying contained; today the same two series widening — even modestly, in basis-point terms — is the opposite signal, and it's the kind of move that eventually shows up in corporate borrowing costs, CD rates, and bond funds if it continues (Concept, below).
history_html:
Today's lead historical fact is about persistence, not a new extreme. The 30-year Treasury yield (5.24%) first touched this level on July 31 and has sat there on 68 of the 81 sessions since — not a one-day spike — last matched broadly, before this run, in July 2007, just before the 2007-09 crisis began in earnest. The 10-year TIPS real yield tells a similar story: first reached today's 2.79% on September 24, held there on 23 of 42 sessions since, last comparable before this run in November 2008. TIPS only go back to 2003, so that needs its cross-check: the Cleveland Fed's model real rate (1982+) puts real rates at the 81st percentile of the last 30 years but only the 54th since 1982 — high against recent decades, ordinary against the full post-1982 record.

The 2007 overlap invites a direct check, so the then-vs-now panel runs it. Several pieces of today's rate structure do sit close to July 2007's: the 10-year yield (4.85% vs. 5.16% then), the 2s10s/3m10y curve shapes, the real yield, the term premium, and Baa−10Y credit spreads are all in range of their 2007 levels. Two things differ meaningfully: the policy-rate anchor is much lower now (SOFR 3.94% vs. fed funds 5.22% then, a 128bp gap), and inflation expectations are calmer (breakeven 2.12% vs. 2.41% then). A different cycle that landed on similar long-end pricing, not a rerun of 2007 — the resemblance is the curve's shape, not what's driving it.

For Jacob at the table: when a client says “30-year rates feel like 2007 again,” the long end genuinely does look similar — but today's starting rate level and inflation backdrop are both friendlier than right before the last crisis, which matters for how far that resemblance should be pushed.

Earnings/guidance reactions and the day's AI-capex-financing-cycle news are prioritized per §5; Oracle's credit story and HP's earnings aftermath are covered for that reason. Also qualifying, left out under the cap: CHTR (+8.39%), AXON (+7.43%), CDW (+6.58%), ADI (+6.44%), EXE (+5.75%), LRCX (−5.68%), BG (+4.87%), IP (+4.77%), TXN (+4.55%), MU (−4.53%), DE (+4.44%), EQT (+4.38%), DDOG (−4.31%), J (−4.27%), SW (+4.25%), CSGP (+4.23%), PWR (−4.10%), WST (−4.07%), UHS (+4.02%), NVDA (−3.91%), AMAT (−3.89%), META (+3.40%), IBM (+3.33%), AMZN (−3.12%), DIS (+2.52%) — none asserted to lack a catalyst, simply not individually researched given the cap.

Oracle (ORCL) −5.13% (103.88, from 109.50) — what happened: fell sharply as its credit stress deepened. Stated reason: per BigGo Finance and Webull, both citing S&P Global Market Intelligence data, Oracle's five-year credit-default-swap spread hit a record of roughly 356 basis points overnight — more than four times where it traded a year ago — as bond investors continue pricing the company's debt-funded AI-datacenter buildout closer to speculative grade; its notes due 2031 reportedly priced to yield near 18%. Read-through: Tier 3-relevant, and the most significant AI-capex-financing-cycle datapoint of the day. This is a financing-structure signal, not a demand one — nothing here says AI spending itself is slowing, only that the market's willingness to keep funding the buildout on favorable terms is visibly straining.

HP Inc (HPQ) +11.49% (31.15, from 27.94) — what happened: rallied sharply the session after reporting fiscal Q4 2026 results. Stated reason: per StockTitan, GuruFocus, and an Investing.com earnings-call transcript, HP beat Q4 estimates on both lines (non-GAAP EPS $0.83 vs. roughly $0.75 consensus; revenue $16.0B vs. roughly $15.43B consensus, +9% y/y) but had initially fallen about 3% the day of the report itself on cautious fiscal 2027 guidance ($3.15–$3.45 EPS) and rising memory-cost pressure, now roughly 40% of HP's PC bill-of-materials per BigGo Finance; no distinct new catalyst was found for today's further move, which reads as the market digesting the beat after that initial guidance-driven dip rather than a fresh announcement. Read-through: Tier 3-adjacent — HP's own disclosure that memory now eats roughly 40% of its PC cost structure is a direct read on AI-driven DRAM/NAND demand spilling into consumer-hardware margins, exactly the kind of cross-market evidence the capex-cycle watch exists to catch.

Sector note — Materials (XLB) +2.07% vs. S&P 500 −0.29%, a 2.36pp divergence. No single named-source catalyst was confirmed for today specifically. The move is consistent with — but not confirmed as — money rotating out of today's chip/tech weakness and into cyclicals; several materials and industrial names qualified individually on today's scan (Deere +4.44%, International Paper +4.77%, Bunge +4.87%, EQT +4.38%, listed above), which is suggestive but not a tested claim (§4C).

The day's dominant financing-cycle news, though, is credit, not demand: Oracle's five-year CDS spread hit a record of roughly 356bp overnight, more than four times where it traded a year ago, as bond investors continue pricing Oracle's debt-funded AI-datacenter buildout closer to speculative grade (Movers, above). On the Minsky-type ladder taught in Unit 7, this is a speculative/vendor-financing-lever story, not a demand-side one — nothing here says hyperscaler AI spending itself is slowing, only that the market's price for funding it on current terms is rising. Cycle-level only; no position-level view (§8).

concept_unit: Unit 3 — Credit spreads, segment 4 reinforcement (R), part two
concept_title: The same test, a different answer — OAS confirms this time
concept_html:
Yesterday's segment ran a simple test on a concentrated chip-sector selloff: when stocks fall hard, check the extra yield lenders demand on junk and investment-grade borrowers (HY and IG OAS) before deciding whether it's a genuine risk event. Yesterday the test said no — both eased on their Monday-dated prints even as Analog Devices, Hewlett Packard Enterprise, and Micron all fell double digits. The lesson wasn't “credit never matters” — it was “check it fresh each morning.” Today, the same cap-weighted/narrow pattern repeated (the S&P 500 and Nasdaq fell again while small-caps and the equal-weight average rose), but the test flipped: HY OAS rose 9bp to 3.72% and IG OAS rose 1bp to 0.98% on their Tuesday-dated prints — small moves in basis-point terms, but enough, against a historically tight 120-day range, to push both to among the highest readings of the past six months, and HY OAS's own three-year record now sits at its 95th percentile.

Why this matters: nine basis points doesn't sound like much next to a multi-percent stock move, but credit spreads move in a much narrower band than stock prices, so a small move there can carry more informational weight than a large one in equities. Today's answer is the opposite of yesterday's — not because the model changed its mind, but because the data did. That's the whole discipline: re-run the test every morning, don't recycle yesterday's conclusion.
client_translation: A rough day for chip stocks plus credit spreads actually widening this time — unlike yesterday — is a more serious combination, worth treating differently from yesterday's wobble even though the stock-price pattern looks almost identical.
client_lens_html:
“Did you see Oracle? Is the AI bubble bursting?” Oracle's cost of insuring its own debt against default hit a record overnight, more than four times where it stood a year ago (Movers, above). That's a real, attributed signal — worth naming plainly as a financing-cost story (can the AI buildout keep getting funded on today's terms), not as a verdict on whether AI demand itself is slowing; those are two different questions, and today's data only speaks to the first one.

“HP jumped 11%? I thought PC companies were struggling with memory costs.” Both things are true at once: HP beat its own earnings estimate but guided cautiously because memory chips now eat roughly 40% of what it costs to build a PC, and the stock still rallied hard the next session once the initial guidance-driven dip had been digested (Movers, above) — a good reminder that a stock's first-day reaction to earnings isn't always its last word.

“What about that inflation and growth data this week?” Core PCE (the Fed's preferred inflation gauge) printed right in line with expectations, and Q3 GDP growth was revised up sharply — strong growth, calm inflation, and neither one clearly explains today's credit-market wobble (Claims, above). Worth saying plainly: this week's chip-sector story and this week's economic data are, so far, two separate things.
